counterexample: The failing inference in line 0024 is: 'chi(Gbar)=3 and chi(boundary(G))<=3 imply chi(G)=3', i.e. that 3-colourability of the interior arrangement subgraph plus 3-colourability of the boundary cycle suffices for 3-colourability of the whole graph G. G is NOT the disjoint union of Gbar and boundary(G): every chord endpoint on the circle is joined by an arc to the first intersection point along that chord, and these cross edges are never constrained by either colouring. The inference is therefore of the form 'G[A] and G[B] are 3-colourable, V(G)=A u B, hence G is 3-colourable', which is false. Explicit witness (7 vertices, 10 edges, planar): A = {a1,a2,a3}, B = {b1,b2,b3,b4}; edges a1a2, a1a3, a2a3 (triangle), b1b2, b2b3, b3b4, b4b1 (4-cycle), and cross edges b1a1, b1a2, b1a3. Check of the two hypotheses: G[A] is a triangle, chi = 3 (colouring a1=1, a2=2, a3=3) -- this plays the role of Gbar with chi=3; G[B] is the 4-cycle b1b2b3b4, chi = 2 <= 3 (colouring b1=b3=1, b2=b4=2) -- this plays the role of the even boundary cycle partial(G), for which the proof's own line 0026 only ever establishes chi <= 3. Check of the failure: {a1,a2,a3,b1} induces K4 (a1a2, a1a3, a2a3, b1a1, b1a2, b1a3 are all present), so chi(G) >= 4; and 4 colours suffice (a1=1, a2=2, a3=3, b1=4, b2=1, b3=2, b4=1: b2 sees b1=4 and b3=2; b3 sees b2=1 and b4=1; b4 sees b3=2 and b1=4), so chi(G) = 4 exactly. Planarity does not rescue the step either: draw the triangle a1a2a3, place b1 in its outer face joined to all three corners, and attach the path b1-b2-b3-b4-b1 outside; no edges cross, so G is planar with both 'parts' 3-colourable yet chi(G)=4. Hence the 'It suffices' of line 0024 is a non sequitur, and the same gap is what makes the arrangement case unproved: for n=3 pairwise-crossing chords, Gbar is the interior triangle (chi=3) and partial(G) is a 6-cycle (chi=2), but G additionally contains 6 cross arcs joining each of the 6 boundary vertices to an interior triangle vertex, and the proof never shows that a 3-colouring of the triangle and a 3-colouring of the 6-cycle can be chosen simultaneously compatible across those arcs. (The proof's own line 0001 concedes exactly this objection.)
reasoning_summary: Lines 0007-0023 are setup and definitions and are unobjectionable. Line 0024's first two claims are acceptable: chi(G)>2 because G contains triangles (e.g. for two crossing chords G is the wheel on a 4-cycle, whose spokes plus a boundary arc form a triangle), and chi(Gbar)=3 is quoted from Felsner-Hurtado-Noy-Streinu. The step fails at the third claim of line 0024: 'It suffices to show that chi(partial G)=3 in order to establish that G is 3-colourable.' Gbar and partial(G) together cover V(G) but omit the arcs joining each chord endpoint on the circle to the nearest interior intersection point, so no combination argument is available; 3-colourability of two vertex-covering subgraphs never implies 3-colourability of the union. The witness above (triangle plus 4-cycle plus three cross edges creating a K4) has both parts 3-colourable and chromatic number 4, and is planar, so no planarity side condition saves the inference. Everything downstream inherits the gap: line 0026 in fact only shows chi(partial G)<=3, which is vacuous since partial(G) is a 2n-cycle of even length and hence 2-colourable outright, so line 0026 supplies no information about G at all. The text's own line 0001 retracts the argument for precisely this reason.
